clinicalPearls: C7 is a terminal complement component required for membrane attack complex assembly, so its deficiency produces recurrent or severe neisserial infection much like other terminal-pathway defects.
Recurrent meningococcal disease, frequently due to non-epidemic serogroups, is the classic presentation and is clinically indistinguishable from C6 deficiency without specific component testing.
Total haemolytic complement (CH50/CH100) is undetectable or markedly reduced, and the alternative-pathway assay (AH50) is likewise abnormal because C7 is shared by both pathways' terminal steps.
Disseminated gonococcal infection and, in some series, an association with certain vasculitic or connective-tissue features have been reported, though neisserial infection dominates.
Combined subtotal C6/C7 deficiency exists because the C6 and C7 genes lie close together on the same chromosome.
Onset of invasive infection is typically in later childhood or adolescence, and recurrences can continue into adulthood.
Meningococcal, pneumococcal and Haemophilus vaccination plus prompt treatment of febrile illness form the mainstay of management.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so at-risk relatives should be screened with a haemolytic complement assay.
reference.pathophysiology: Complement Component 7 deficiency results from biallelic loss-of-function variants in the C7 gene, which encodes a terminal complement protein. C7 binds the C5b-6 complex to form C5b-7, a critical hydrophobic intermediate that inserts into the target membrane and provides the platform for subsequent binding of C8 and polymerising C9, completing the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9). Absence of functional C7 halts MAC assembly at the C5b-6 stage, abolishing complement-dependent direct bacteriolysis while leaving opsonisation and anaphylatoxin production from the upstream cascade intact. Because Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are killed principally by MAC-mediated serum bactericidal activity, patients are disproportionately susceptible to invasive meningococcal disease and disseminated gonococcal infection. The C7 gene is physically linked to C6, and shared regulatory or structural variants can produce combined or subtotal deficiencies. The remainder of innate and adaptive immunity is preserved, which explains why susceptibility is largely restricted to neisserial organisms.
additionalDifferentials: C6 deficiency, which is clinically identical and distinguished only by component assay
C8 deficiency (alpha-gamma or beta subunit) with comparable neisserial risk
C5 deficiency, which additionally impairs C5a-driven chemotaxis
C9 deficiency, generally a milder terminal defect
Properdin deficiency presenting with fulminant meningococcaemia
Functional or anatomical asplenia predisposing to encapsulated organisms
Antibody deficiency syndromes causing recurrent bacterial infection
additionalInvestigations: CH50/CH100 classical-pathway haemolytic screen as the first-line test
AH50 alternative-pathway assay to confirm a shared terminal-component block
Specific C7 antigenic and functional measurement to identify the deficient protein
C7 gene sequencing to define the variant and detect combined C6/C7 defects
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid culture with meningococcal serogrouping during acute infection
Assay of the other terminal components (C5, C6, C8, C9) to exclude combined deficiency
Haemolytic complement screening of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Second or subsequent episode of invasive meningococcal disease
Neisserial infection with an unusual or non-epidemic serogroup
Family history of recurrent or fatal meningococcal infection
Fever with meningism or a purpuric rash in a patient known to be C7 deficient
Persistently undetectable CH50/CH100 when not acutely consuming complement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable when infections are recognised and treated promptly and when vaccination is kept up to date; as with other terminal defects, invasive neisserial disease tends to be less fulminant than in the general population. The dominant long-term concern is recurrent infection, making sustained prophylaxis and rapid access to care important.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate the complement system after invasive neisserial infection, particularly with rare serogroups or recurrence.
Measuring only C6 or only C7 and missing a combined C6/C7 deficiency owing to the genes' proximity.
Interpreting a low CH50 from a degraded or mishandled specimen as a true deficiency.
Assuming vaccination confers absolute protection and lowering vigilance for breakthrough infection.
Neglecting to counsel and screen relatives once the proband is identified.
references: Standard clinical immunology textbook, current edition
National immunisation guidance for complement-deficient and asplenic patients
Peer-reviewed reviews of terminal complement deficiency and neisserial infection
management: Immunise against meningococcus with quadrivalent conjugate (ACWY) and serogroup B vaccines with scheduled boosters to offset absent membrane-attack-complex activity.
Maintain pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination.
Treat any fever urgently with empirical antibiotics active against Neisseria and obtain cultures with serogrouping.
Consider long-term prophylactic penicillin where infections recur.
Educate patient and family to seek immediate care for possible meningococcal disease.
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and screen relatives, testing for combined C6/C7 deficiency given the adjacent gene loci.
